Mayor Brandon Johnson proposes funding mental health clinics using litigated social media tax revenue as federal ARPA funds expire.
Chicago Mental Health Budget Plan
Evidence: Clinic Reopenings, Litigated Tax Revenue, Unfunded Mandates
#Chicago #MentalHealth 🌐

Mayor Johnson's 2027 budget proposal promises permanent funding for the CARE crisis intervention program and reopens city-run mental health clinics by tapping revenue from a disputed social media tax.
Stated Judgement: (+0.82, +0.72) — Greater Good

The proposed funding hinges on $49.2M tied up in litigation escrow, while expiring federal ARPA funds leave CARE at risk. Furthermore, the budget lacks specific locations, dates, or cost estimates for the proposed clinic.
Resulting Judgement: (+0.06, +0.09) — Greater Good

Verdict: PASS — Fall from Grace.
Integrity: Severe Deception (Hypocrisy: 14.20, z: 4)

- Chicago Sun-Times: COND (-0.68, -0.52) — Repeats escrowed tax claims without funding guarantees.
- ABC News TAS: PASS (+0.80, +0.70) — Clear factual report on hospital arson plea.

Chicago's 2027 budget seeks $5M to sustain CARE crisis teams as federal pandemic relief ends. However, relying on an escrowed 50-cent social media tax leaves municipal mental health infrastructure vulnerable to court challenges.

The Bright Side:
The CARE program has expanded operating hours to 14 hours daily and built community trust, proving that non-police 911 mental health response models are physically effective when adequately staffed.

The Breakdown & Plane Error:
The city commits a Plane 5 (Logical) vs Plane 3 (Physical) substitution by treating litigated escrow revenues as guaranteed physical operating capital, mistaking legal speculation for deliverable healthcare access.

Social Physics Analysis:
Mayor Johnson executes a Smart Selfish Maneuver by claiming credit for expanding mental health infrastructure while offloading fiscal risk onto uncollected tax litigation. Speculative revenue substitutes for guaranteed funding.

The Trajectory: The Path of Fall from Grace.
Modal Dynamics: will be -> can't be via Red Top (The Imperial Trap).
By pitching universal delivery while relying on constrained legal escrow, the policy collapses potential service into bureaucratic standstill.

The Unavoidable Truth: Public mental health crisis response requires guaranteed municipal funding to survive federal sunsets.
The Unavoidable Lie: Disputed tax dollars locked in escrow constitute a real fiscal foundation for community care.

Alethekanon:
Budgeting public healthcare on escrowed litigation revenue creates structural fragility. Real institutional capacity requires balance-sheet reality, not conditional accounting promises.

Awwthekanon:
People experiencing mental health crises need reliable, compassionate care and safe spaces. Tying their lifeline to tax lawsuits leaves vulnerable neighbors waiting in uncertainty.

Brothekanon:
Bro, promising to open new clinics with money stuck in court escrow is like buying a sports car with a lottery ticket you haven't won yet.

Spirithekanon:
"Which of you, intending to build a tower, does not first sit down and count the cost, whether he has enough to complete it?" Luke 14:28 FAIL
Promising public health facilities on uncollected legal claims violates fundamental fiscal stewardship.

Mayor Brandon Johnson speaks Oct. 2 during a news conference announcing the expansion of the Community Assistance and Recovery Engagement program’s hours of operation at the Lawndale Mental Health Center. He recently announced plans to lean on funds generated from the social media tax to create permanent city funding for the program.

Octavio Jones/For the Sun-Times

Share

Mayor Brandon Johnson’s 2027 budget proposes using city funds to reopen a community mental health clinic and create permanent funding for the Crisis Assistance Response and Engagement program.

Johnson plans to announce the city’s investments in mental health services Wednesday during the unveiling of his 2027 budget. The investment will include $5 million to make CARE, which dispatches a mental health team to certain 911 calls, a permanent city program, Johnson said.

“I’ve made a commitment to ensure that people can receive treatment that they need, and this is a direct investment to bolster our work around community safety,” Johnson said in an interview with the Chicago Sun-Times/WBEZ this week.

He said the investment to reopen another mental health clinic is part of his promise to reverse the city’s past actions of shuttering community clinics. Between 1989 and 2012, the city closed 14 mental health clinics, leaving only five in place by 2016, according to a 2025 audit of the city’s mental health equity initiative. Johnson did not provide specifics about where the mental health clinic would open in 2027 or how much it could cost.

He plans to lean on funds allocated to the groundbreaking and controversial social media tax, which collects 50 cents per Chicago user after the first 100,000 users.

The city has collected more funds than anticipated from social media companies, and it’s on pace to collect $49.2 million by the end of the year. But those funds are being held in escrow pending litigation on the tax. Still, Johnson said he’s confident the city will prevail in court, especially since the state has since enacted a similar tax.

“We’re pretty confident about our ability to move through the litigation process and have the permanent revenue stream to make sure that we’re protecting our public institutions, and especially mental and behavioral healthcare,” Johnson said.

In recent years, Johnson’s administration reopened city-run mental health clinics in Pilsen and Roseland. In 2025, the city’s budget allocated about $12.2 million for mental health clinics. The city’s larger budget for mental health programming in recent years has leaned heavily on federal funds from the American Rescue Plan Act, according to the 2025 audit.

Johnson’s 2027 budget proposal calls for $5 million for CARE, which is similar to the federal funds allocated for it. About $5.2 million in funds from the American Rescue Plan was allocated for the program, but those federal funds end this year.

“The motivation for me has always been based upon just lived experiences, and the fact that, you know, you had previous administrations that actually shut down mental and behavioral healthcare, right?” Johnson said. “And previous administrations that refused to make these investments. So my motivation is certainly very much connected to the need that is substantial.”

The federal funds were used to staff citywide operations. The teams respond to requests for mental health services via 911 calls or when a dispatcher initiates a CARE response. The program recently expanded its hours from 8 a.m. to 10 p.m., the city previously announced.

Johnson said the city continues to work on building trust for these new services, pointing to an increase in calls for CARE teams.

“The more we make this readily available, I believe that that confidence will continue to grow,” Johnson said.

Woman pleads guilty to arson at mental health unit

A woman who set a fire in a mental health ward in a north-west Tasmanian public hospital has pleaded guilty to arson.

Actual Article Body:

Backstory

Newsletters

中文新闻

BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

TOK PISIN

By Sandy Powell

Topic:Arson

The mental health unit was extensively damaged. (Supplied: Tasmanian government)

The 28-year-old woman who set fire to a Tasmanian hospital's mental health clinic has pleaded guilty to arson.

At the time of the fire, 19 patients were admitted to the clinic, and beds needed to be found elsewhere for them.

The woman will be sentenced before a judge in the Supreme Court.

The woman who set a fire in a mental health ward in a north-west Tasmanian public hospital has pleaded guilty to arson.

The 28-year-old appeared before Magistrate Katie Edwards via video link from prison in the Burnie Magistrates Court, charged with one count of arson.

No facts of the case were heard in court, and the matter was adjourned for facts and sentencing before a Supreme Court Judge in December.

The fire broke out in the Spencer Clinic at the North West Regional Hospital in Burnie on September 19.

Emergency crews were called to the hospital about 6:30 that night, and it took firefighters several hours to contain the blaze, which caused significant damage.

The following day, Tasmania Police said they had charged a 28-year-old woman with arson, and she had been remanded in custody to appear in court.

Today was the woman's second appearance before a magistrate.

Nineteen people were admitted to the unit at the time of the fire. (Supplied: Tasmanian government)

At the outset of proceedings, Tasmania Legal Aid lawyer Claire Willis indicated she would be entering pleas of guilty to the charge on her client's behalf.

Magistrate Edwards asked the woman to sign copies of the plea that had been provided to her in prison, before adjourning the matter to the Supreme Court for facts and sentence by a judge.

At the time of the fire, 19 patients were admitted to the Spencer Clinic, and beds needed to be found elsewhere in Tasmanian hospitals for them.

Earlier in October, Health Minister Bridget Archer said most of the capacity of the clinic would return in November, but part of the building would need to be demolished.

Construction work is underway to reopen 10 private rooms in the remaining portion of the building, and a further eight beds elsewhere on the hospital campus will soon be available.

For several years the Tasmanian government has been planning to build a new, 22-bed dedicated mental health facility at the hospital.

The government has budgeted $40 million for the facility and said earlier this month it had awarded a tender for its construction, which it said would be completed in 2028.
